title: The W-2 and 1099 mailing guide: how to get year-end tax forms from approved file to mailbox
summary: Prepare for W-2 and 1099 deadlines with a tax-season checklist for secure printing, recipient mailing, peak capacity and outsourced mail production.
body_markdown:
The payroll file is approved. The forms are generated. The deadline is on the calendar. Yet thousands of W-2s and 1099s may still be waiting to be printed, inserted, addressed and mailed.


For many organizations, tax season creates one of the busiest periods of the year for mail operations. Large volumes of time-sensitive documents need to be prepared and sent within a short window, often alongside everyday statements, notices and other business correspondence.


And getting those forms into the mail isn't just another operational task. For W-2s, a correctly addressed form mailed by the applicable deadline generally satisfies the IRS furnishing requirement. That makes the mailing process an important part of meeting your organization's tax-reporting obligations.


But even the best-laid plans can run into challenges. Equipment failures, staffing shortages, last-minute address corrections or unexpected volume spikes can all put mailing schedules at risk. Having a[business continuity plan](https://www.pitneybowes.com/us/blog/what-true-business-continuity-looks-like.html) in place can help keep critical communications moving when something unexpected happens.


This guide walks through five practical steps to get your year-end tax forms from approved file to mailbox, helping your payroll, HR, finance, IT and mail operations teams stay organized and avoid last-minute disruptions.


## **Step 1: Know what you’re mailing and when (6–8 weeks out)**


Being mail-ready starts with knowing your deadline and your volume.


For many common forms, January 31 is the standard recipient deadline in the year following the tax year. Not every form uses the same date, though, and weekends or holidays can move the deadline to the next business day. Always confirm the applicable year and form instructions.\[1\]\[2\]


**Form**


**Typical recipient deadline**


**What operations should know**


W-2


January 31 (generally)


Employee copies must be furnished. A correctly addressed W-2 mailed by the applicable deadline generally satisfies the IRS furnishing rule.


1099-NEC


January 31 (generally)


Recipient copies and IRS filing follow the early deadline; the two workflows are distinct.


1099-MISC


Generally January 31; certain statements February 15


Deadlines vary by reportable box and form type. Check the applicable instructions.


One distinction trips up many teams: filing is not furnishing. Businesses filing 10 or more information returns in aggregate generally must file electronically with the government unless an exception applies. That does not eliminate the need to deliver recipient statements, and electronic W-2 furnishing has its own employee-consent requirements.\[3\]\[4\] Review the SSA employer filing guidance and the IRS rules on electronic W-2 delivery before you settle on your mix of paper and electronic distribution.\[5\]


**Use this step to make three decisions:**


- Confirm form types, recipient deadlines and projected piece counts.
- Name an owner for each step across payroll, HR, finance, IT and mail operations.
- Decide how the mail will be produced, because that choice shapes every step that follows.


**Choosing the right print and mail approach.** Most organizations size their print and mail operation for a typical week, not a concentrated year-end batch. W-2s, 1099s, benefit statements, billing notices and everyday customer mail can all arrive together, competing for the same people and equipment. You have three practical options, and you don’t need to use the same one for every mailing:


If your team is evaluating how to manage seasonal demand, these[tips for overcoming common mail center challenges](https://www.pitneybowes.com/us/blog/avoid-mail-center-challenges.html) can help identify opportunities to improve efficiency without adding permanent resources.


**Keep it in-house with a backup ready** : If your process generally works, prearrange an alternate production path for the jobs that can’t wait. A staffing gap or equipment failure then doesn’t turn into an emergency vendor search.


**Go hybrid** : Keep everyday mail onsite and route tax-season batches, year-end notices or overflow to an established digital print and mail partner. This reduces the pressure to buy equipment or add permanent staff for a short annual peak.


**Outsource fully** : An external provider handles print, assembly and mailing, including recurring communications. Your team continues to own content, recipient accuracy, approvals and applicable legal obligations.


If a partner is on the table, evaluate as soon as possible to be prepared by the time the season comes around. Look for:


- Secure file submission, access controls and a clear handling process for sensitive recipient data.
- Proof of capacity for concentrated jobs alongside normal business mail.
- Test-file reviews, controlled versions and documented quality checks.
- Production and mail piece visibility, exception handling and traceable reporting.
- Clear handoff responsibilities, service commitments and contingency procedures.
- Experience with presort and ways to evaluate total print, preparation and postage costs.


## **Step 2: Make your addresses and files mail-ready (3–4 weeks out)**


Even accurate tax forms can run into mailing delays.


Incorrect or outdated addresses, inconsistent file formats and late employee changes create rework just when production windows are tightest. Assign one owner to manage corrections and maintain a single approved version of each file.


**This step’s checkpoints:**


- Validate recipient addresses and data feeds.
- Confirm approved forms, inserts and envelopes.
- Agree on how late changes will be handled once the file is locked.


W-2 envelopes are not marketing space. The IRS restricts logos, slogans and advertising on employee W-2 copies and the envelopes that contain them, with limited exceptions. Have your compliance team approve the form and envelope design before production.\[6\]


## **Step 3: Keep sensitive mail secure (3–4 weeks out, and throughout)**


Tax forms carry personal and financial information, and at peak they can pass through more hands than any other mailing you produce.


**Security needs to be designed into the mail workflow, not added at the end. Define:**


- Who can access the files, and who can release them to production.
- Where the files are stored and how they are transferred.
- How approved forms and versions are controlled.
- What documentation is retained, and for how long.


Confirm these safeguards with IT and with your production partner. For a broader view of data protection, see the[Pitney Bowes Trust Center](https://www.pitneybowes.com/us/enterprise-shipping-360/trust-center.html) .


## **Step 4: Test the mail run before it counts (1–2 weeks out)**


Run a test to confirm your files, equipment and mailing process are ready.


Run test files and quality checks. Confirm print capacity, presort eligibility, reporting and escalation contacts. Then ask the question that decides whether a minor issue doesn’t become a major delay: if something fails, what is our alternate path to the mailbox?


A printer issue, network outage, office move or unplanned absence can stall a run as surely as a major emergency. With no alternate production path, routine disruption can stop the entire mailing.


## **Step 5: Release the mail, then confirm it went out**


Mailing isn’t finished when the job leaves the building. It’s finished when you can show what went out.


Before release, approve final counts and versions, freeze authorized input files and identify who can release production.


After handoff, reconcile accepted pieces against production status, retain required records and resolve exceptions promptly.


## **Your mail-ready timeline at a glance**


These checkpoints are planning recommendations, not additional IRS-imposed deadlines.


**When to check**


**Action**


6–8 weeks before


Confirm form types, recipient deadlines, projected piece counts, owners and alternate production options.


3–4 weeks before


Validate recipient addresses and data feeds; confirm approved forms, inserts, envelopes and file security.


1–2 weeks before


Run test files and quality checks; confirm print capacity, presort eligibility, reporting and escalation contacts.


Before release


Approve final counts and versions; freeze authorized input files; identify who can release production.


After handoff


Reconcile accepted pieces and production status; retain required records and resolve exceptions promptly.
